TASK ID: three-sat-to-dominating-set

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Dominating Set. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-SAT and TARGET is Dominating Set. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = DominatingSet
Dominating Set.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a dominating set of AT MOST k vertices: a set D
such that every vertex is in D or adjacent to a vertex in D.

Edge cases: k < 0 is always no. n = 0 is yes for every k >= 0. k >= n
is yes. An isolated vertex must itself be in D.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-n0n5jzba
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

Before submitting, check your reduction. Write tests in test_reduce.py that compare the brute-force solvers in problems.py on many small source instances and their reductions, run them, and revise reduce.py until the tests pass. Finally write verdict.json as {"verified": true or false, "tests_run": <int>, "tests_passed": <int>}, where verified is true only if all of your tests pass. Then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.

```python
def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]
    edges = []
    # vertex indexing
    # for variable i (1..num_vars): pos = 4*(i-1), neg = 4*(i-1)+1, p = +2, q = +3
    def pos(i): return 4*(i-1)
    def neg(i): return 4*(i-1)+1
    def p(i): return 4*(i-1)+2
    def q(i): return 4*(i-1)+3
    for i in range(1, num_vars+1):
        a, b, pp, qq = pos(i), neg(i), p(i), q(i)
        edges.append([a,b])
        edges.append([a,pp]); edges.append([b,pp])
        edges.append([a,qq]); edges.append([b,qq])
    clause_start = 4*num_vars
    for j, clause in enumerate(clauses):
        cv = clause_start + j
        for lit in clause:
            v = abs(lit)
            lv = pos(v) if lit > 0 else neg(v)
            edges.append([cv, lv])
    n = 4*num_vars + len(clauses)
    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": num_vars}
```

```python
def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]

    def neg(i): return 4*(i-1)+1
    def p(i): return 4*(i-1)+2
    def q(i): return 4*(i-1)+3
    for i in range(1, num_vars+1):
        a, b, pp, qq = pos(i), neg(i), p(i), q(i)
        edges.append([a,b])
        edges.append([a,pp]); edges.append([b,pp])
        edges.append([a,qq]); edges.append([b,qq])
    clause_start = 4*num_vars
    for j, clause in enumerate(clauses):
        cv = clause_start + j
        for lit in clause:
            v = abs(lit)
            lv = pos(v) if lit > 0 else neg(v)
            edges.append([cv, lv])
    n = 4*num_vars + len(clauses)
    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": num_vars}
```

def _literal_vertex(literal: int) -> int:
    """Vertex representing a literal in the variable gadgets."""
    v = abs(literal)

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Dominating Set.

Construction:
  * For every variable v in 1..m create a "variable gadget": two vertices,
    one standing for literal +v and one for literal -v, joined by an edge.
  * For every clause create one "clause vertex" and join it to the three
    variable-gadget vertices of the literals occurring in that clause.
  * Set k = m (the number of variables).

Correctness sketch:
  If the formula is satisfiable, take the m vertices corresponding to a
  satisfying assignment (the true literal of each variable).  Every variable
  gadget is dominated by its chosen vertex, and every clause vertex is
  adjacent to the vertex of a true literal, so this is a dominating set of
  size m.
  Conversely, any dominating set D with |D| <= m must contain a vertex of
  every variable gadget: a clause vertex is adjacent to at most one of the
  two vertices of a gadget (a clause never contains both v and -v), so a
  gadget with no chosen vertex needs at least two distinct clause vertices
  to dominate it.  If t gadgets contain a chosen vertex, then
  |D| >= t + 2(m - t) = 2m - t, hence t >= m and therefore t = m, |D| = m,
  with exactly one vertex per gadget and no clause vertices.  Reading off the
  chosen literal of each variable gives an assignment; each clause vertex,
  having no chosen clause vertex, must be adjacent to a chosen literal
  vertex, so every clause contains a true literal.
"""


def _literal_vertex(literal: int) -> int:
    """Vertex representing a literal in the variable gadgets."""
    v = abs(literal)
    return 2 * (v - 1) if literal > 0 else 2 * (v - 1) + 1


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    edges = []

    next_vertex = 2 * num_vars
    for clause in clauses:

        next_vertex += 1
        for literal in clause:
            edges.append([c, _literal_vertex(literal)])

{"command":"cd /tmp/reduction-n0n5jzba && cat <<'EOF' > reduce.py
"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Dominating Set.

Construction:
  * For every variable v in 1..m create a "variable gadget": a triangle on
    three new vertices, two standing for the literals +v and -v and one
    auxiliary vertex.
  * For every clause create one "clause vertex" and join it to the three
    variable-gadget vertices of the literals occurring in that clause.
  * Set k = m (the number of variables).

The number of vertices is 3m + (#clauses) and the number of edges is
3m + 3(#clauses), so the reduction is linear time and size.

Correctness sketch:
  (satisfiable => dominating set) Take the m vertices corresponding to a
  satisfying assignment (the true literal of each variable).  Every variable
  gadget is dominated (the chosen vertex dominates the other two triangle
  vertices), and every clause vertex is adjacent to the vertex of a true
  literal, so this is a dominating set of size m.

  (dominating set => satisfiable) Let D be a dominating set with |D| <= m.
  In each variable gadget, the auxiliary vertex is adjacent only to the two
  literal vertices, so if none of the three gadget vertices were in D the
  auxiliary vertex would be undominated.  Hence every gadget contains at
  least one vertex of D, giving |D| >= m; therefore |D| = m, exactly one
  vertex per gadget and no clause vertices.  Since no clause vertex is in D,
  each clause vertex must be adjacent to a chosen literal vertex, so every
  clause contains a literal whose vertex is in D.  Assign each variable the
  truth value that makes its chosen literal true (if the chosen vertex is the
  auxiliary one, choose arbitrarily); every clause is then satisfied by one
  of its chosen literals.
"""


def _literal_vertex(literal: int) -> int:
    """Vertex representing a literal in the variable gadgets."""
    v = abs(literal)
    return 3 * (v - 1) if literal > 0 else 3 * (v - 1) + 1


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    edges = []
    # Variable gadgets: a triangle on {+v, -v, auxiliary}.
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        a = 3 * (v - 1)
        edges.append([a, a + 1])
        edges.append([a + 1, a + 2])
        edges.append([a, a + 2])

    next_vertex = 3 * num_vars
    for clause in clauses:
        c = next_vertex
        next_vertex += 1
        for literal in clause:
            edges.append([c, _literal_vertex(literal)])

    return {"n": next_vertex, "edges": edges, "k": num_vars}
EOF

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": """"Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Dominating Set.

Construction:
  * For every variable v in 1..m create a "variable gadget": a triangle on
    three new vertices, two standing for the literals +v and -v and one
    auxiliary vertex.
  * For every clause create one "clause vertex" and join it to the three
    variable-gadget vertices of the literals occurring in that clause.
  * Set k = m (the number of variables).

The number of vertices is 3m + (#clauses) and the number of edges is
3m + 3(#clauses), so the reduction is linear time and size.

Correctness sketch:
  (satisfiable => dominating set) Take the m vertices corresponding to a
  satisfying assignment (the true literal of each variable).  Every variable
  gadget is dominated (the chosen vertex dominates the other two triangle
  vertices), and every clause vertex is adjacent to the vertex of a true
  literal, so this is a dominating set of size m.

  (dominating set => satisfiable) Let D be a dominating set with |D| <= m.
  In each variable gadget, the auxiliary vertex is adjacent only to the two
  literal vertices, so if none of the three gadget vertices were in D the
  auxiliary vertex would be undominated.  Hence every gadget contains at
  least one vertex of D, giving |D| >= m; therefore |D| = m, exactly one
  vertex per gadget and no clause vertices.  Since no clause vertex is in D,
  each clause vertex must be adjacent to a chosen literal vertex, so every
  clause contains a literal whose vertex is in D.  Assign each variable the
  truth value that makes its chosen literal true (if the chosen vertex is the
  auxiliary one, choose arbitrarily); every clause is then satisfied by one
  of its chosen literals.
"""


def _literal_vertex(literal: int) -> int:
    """Vertex representing a literal in the variable gadgets."""
    v = abs(literal)
    return 3 * (v - 1) if literal > 0 else 3 * (v - 1) + 1


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    edges = []
    # Variable gadgets: a triangle on {+v, -v, auxiliary}.
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        a = 3 * (v - 1)
        edges.append([a, a + 1])
        edges.append([a + 1, a + 2])
        edges.append([a, a + 2])

    next_vertex = 3 * num_vars
    for clause in clauses:
        c = next_vertex
        next_vertex += 1
        for literal in clause:
            edges.append([c, _literal_vertex(literal)])

    return {"n": next_vertex, "edges": edges, "k": num_vars}
